>> This message comes from Odoo.
Running a business shouldn't feel like surviving a software group project.
Start managing your business with one unified system.
Odoo is the all-in-one business management software.
Try for free today at odoo.com/nprpodcasts.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Roman.
>> Days after congressional Republicans sustained big defeats in the midterm elections,
President Trump is replacing his White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller.
Miller is the deputy chief of staff and the architect of many of the president's most controversial policies,
including the stepped-up immigration enforcement efforts.
As he departed for Florida, the president briefly spoke to reporters at the White House.
>> Stephen Miller will be the new chief of staff, and Susie's going to go over to the political operation.
>> What do you want Stephen Miller to do to get what he needs to do?
>> Just run things well.
>> Democrats in Congress are reacting to the news.
Minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, who was widely expected to be the next speaker of the House in January,
said, "Miller has blood on his hands, and his presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.
Fire him now."
In a close race, Republican Congressman Jeff Hurd has won re-election in Congress from Colorado.
He could be the only Republican in the state's congressional delegation.
Colorado Public Radio's Steena Stig reports.
>> Hurd was touring flood damage in the southwest part of the state when he learned he had won Colorado's third congressional district,
fending off Democratic challenger Dwayne Romero.
It was an election dominated by Democrats.
>> I think there's a message for us as Republicans that we need to make sure we are focused on what we need to focus on,
and that's making sure that we're making life better for families in western southern Colorado.
>> Recent floods have damaged hundreds of homes in Hurd's district.
He and the rest of Colorado's congressional delegation have signed a letter requesting federal disaster relief.
For NPR News, I'm Steena Stig in Grand Junction, Colorado.
>> Employers in the United States added 165,000 jobs in October.
It was far more than analysts were expecting.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports.
>> A new report from the Labor Department shows significantly stronger job growth than forecasters had expected for October.
Job gains for August and September were also revised up.
Industries adding jobs last month include health care, transportation, and professional services.
Restaurants cut workers in October, as did construction companies.
The unemployment rate inched down to 4.1 percent, even as hundreds of thousands of new people joined the workforce.
The stronger job market also shows up in bigger wage gains.
Average wages in October were up 3.1 percent from a year ago.
That's a bigger annual increase than the previous month, but still probably not enough to keep pace with rising prices.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
>> Wall Street closed the week with a mixed market after Thursday's big sell-off.
The Dow was down, but the NASDAQ and the S&P were up.
This is NPR News.
Soft robots might one day squeeze into crevices that explore shipwrecks and conduct research and research operations.
As Ari Daniel reports, the researchers are studying the octopus as a source of their inspiration.
Aside from a rigid capsule around the brain and a small hard beak used for eating, the octopus is entirely deformable.
>> People are fascinated by the escape artist aspect of octopuses.
>> Vienna Zoo biologist Tamar Gutnik and her colleagues observed octopuses transiting through different sized holes.
The animals consistently inserted a single arm and then a few more.
They then used those arms to pull the rest of the body across.
With small holes, the common octopus compressed its body cavity and internal organs to squeeze through.
Next up is the difficult task of building a robot that mimics the behavior of the octopuses.
For NPR News, I'm Ari Daniel.
>> The twin ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach are facing a midnight Pacific time deadline to reach a contract agreement with an estimated 250 union security guards.
The current contract has been extended while the management group, the Pacific Maritime Association and the ILWU negotiate with the help of a federal mediator.
A strike could have a big impact on the U.S. economy as unionized workers in other bargaining units are expected to honor the picket lines if they go up,
and it comes at a critical time as retailers are getting ready for the holiday shopping season.
I'm Dan Ronan, NPR News in Washington.
